newsitem.title: USA: Implantable heart-shocker saves lives - study.
newsitem.headline: Implantable heart-shocker saves lives - study.

text.p: A five-year study of conventional drugs and an implantable device that delivers electric shocks to a heart with an erratic beat has shown the device may cut the death rate by half among heart attack survivors.
The findings, published in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine, are controversial because the heart-shocker devices are expensive and there are reasons to question the study's conclusions.

Nonetheless, the results are significant because each year 16,000 Americans develop the type of heart problem treated by the research team, led by Dr. Arthur J. Moss of the University of Rochester School of Medicine and Dentistry.

The condition, known as unsustained ventricular tachycardia, is found in people who have survived a heart attack with a permanent scar on the main pumping chamber of their heart and leads to death in about 30 percent of patients within two years.
The Moss study was an attempt to determine whether the implantable devices, known as defibrillators, are more effective than conventional drugs at preventing the heart from adopting a fatal rhythm.
In the study, 95 volunteers got the defibrillators and 101 received conventional drug treatment.

Fifteen people in the defibrillator group died during the study -- 11 of whom succumbed to heart problems. In contrast, 39 people receiving conventional therapy died, 27 from heart attacks or other signs of heart disease.

But the medical community should not rush to embrace the implications of the findings, according to an editorial in the Journal by Dr. Peter L. Friedman and William G. Stevenson of Brigham and Women's Hospital in Boston.

"Using hospital charges and physicians' fees at Brigham and Women's Hospital as a model, we estimate that the cost of identifying, evaluating, and implanting cardioverter-defibrillators in these 16,000 patients would be over $1 billion annually, not including the cost of follow-up evaluations every three months after implantation," they said.

Friedman and Stevenson also said that when the study began in 1991, doctors were giving drugs that were later found to increase the risk of death. After doctors became aware of that problem and stopped using those drugs, the death rate among both groups in the Moss study became similar.
In other words, the defibrillators may not be more beneficial than conventional treatment.

In this day and age, "an annual mortality rate of 8 to 10 percent would be expected" among patients involved in the Moss study, they said. "Such a survival rate is similar to that in the group that received implantable cardioverter-defibrillators."
